prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks, which brought atomic timekeeping to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks satisfy the discovery-or-invention test cleanly. Katori's magic-wavelength proposal is a single identifiable idea, and it was turned into operating clocks whose systematic uncertainty is now near 1e-18 and agrees across several independent laboratories. The consequences are concrete and measurable: tests of fundamental constants, relativistic geodesy and the coming redefinition of the second. It is the only candidate that all eight of us ranked, and it has two first places (Kroll, Lindroth) and a second-ranked precision-measurement specialist in Lindroth who can judge the atomic-structure details directly. A two-name configuration is compact and leaves no real dispute between the proposer of the concept and the group that drove the accuracy frontier. Moving my own first choice, B009, down to an alternative is deliberate: I am too close to that field to press it as the committee's lead candidate on the strength of my ranking alone.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that this can be read as a continuation of the 2005 frequency-comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize rather than a new discovery, and a committee wary of rewarding the same lineage a third time could reasonably wait. The second reservation is that the SI second has not yet been redefined, so one could argue the full payoff is still prospective. Attribution is also not airtight: Lemonde, Gill, Lisdat and the Yb and ion-clock groups made real contributions that a two-name credit leaves out. I regard these as qualifications on the citation wording and not as reasons to withhold recognition, but they would count more if a stronger and cleaner candidate emerged.

responses.point: Circuit QED (B016) is highly mature, defines the architecture of nearly every superconducting processor, and has a clean theory-plus-two-experiments allocation among Blais, Wallraff and Schoelkopf, with only a mild risk of looking too close to the 2025 prize.
responses.response: I ranked B016 second and agree on the science and on the allocation, which is the cleanest of any candidate on the list. My disagreement is about sequencing, not merit. Danielsson, Eriksson and Kroll each flagged proximity to the 2025 circuit prize, and I think that concern is stronger than 'mild': a second circuit-based prize in two years would need an argument that the architecture is a distinct discovery and not an enabling technology for the same community. You also say you direct a related centre and may be biased, which I respect, but it means your own estimate of that overlap risk is the one I trust least. I keep B016 as my first alternative and would support it if the committee judges the overlap acceptable.

responses.point: Optical lattice clocks opened a new regime of precision measurement, the two-name configuration is natural, and the 2005 and 2012 prizes covered only the neighbouring comb and ion-trap advances, so recognition is timely and arguably overdue.
responses.response: I agree and I rely on your judgement of the atomic-structure side, which is outside my own training. I want to qualify one thing: you call the neighbouring prizes 'neighbouring', but Kroll, Danielsson and Eriksson all list overlap with them as their main doubt, so the case should say explicitly what is new. My answer is that the magic-wavelength condition is a distinct invention that makes many-atom interrogation compatible with a narrow clock transition, and the 1e-18 systematic budget is a different instrument from the single-ion clock. If you can also confirm from the physics that lattice clocks are the leading route to the redefinition rather than one of several, I would be more comfortable with the citation.

responses.point: Aberration-corrected TEM (B009) is fully mature and overdue, with an established and apparently uncontested Rose, Haider, Urban configuration, though Krivanek's STEM corrector is a notable parallel line and the physics-versus-materials-instrument question remains.
responses.response: Thank you for ranking it sixth and for the fair reading of the attribution. I should be plain that I ranked it first as a specialist in the field and that I am the wrong person to be its main advocate. Your Krivanek point is the serious one: Krivanek and Dellby's STEM corrector was a parallel achievement, and I would not call the credit uncontested, which is why I do not think B009 is ready as a three-name prize. Kroll's doubt about whether an instrument prize fits the physics category is also fair after the 1986 Ruska precedent. Given modest support (Pearce 6, Kroll 7) and my own proximity, I have moved it to the alternatives and not pressed it as the lead.

responses.point: Twisted bilayer graphene (B024) is a rare case of a continuum-model prediction of a magic-angle flat band followed by a decisive experiment, widely reproduced, though the pairing mechanism is still debated and recognition may be early.
responses.response: I ranked B024 fourth and the theory-plus-experiment story is compelling. My concern is the one you partly share: the superconducting mechanism and many correlated phases are unresolved, and Lindroth, Mehlig and Pearce also call recognition somewhat early. Mehlig adds that the first author, Yuan Cao, is outside the credited names, which I take as a real attribution problem for the experimental share. I would not choose it this year, but I would want it kept on the shortlist for a later cycle, when the physics has settled and the credit boundary is clearer.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will treat lattice clocks as distinct enough from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes.
Whether the two-name credit adequately covers Lemonde, Lisdat and the Yb and ion-clock contributors.
Whether the 2025 circuit prize makes B016 too close, since that decides how B016 and B031 rank against each other.
Whether the Krivanek STEM corrector line should be credited alongside the TEM corrector in B009, and whether instrument prizes in electron microscopy count as physics for this committee.
statement.conflict_note: I work in transmission electron microscopy and am president of the International Federation of Societies for Microscopy, so B009 is my own field and I would want to recuse myself from its decision, which is one reason I do not make it my preferred choice. I do not know of a personal tie to Rose, Urban or Haider from the provided profile. I hold a University of Tokyo fellowship and have long-running exchanges with Japanese universities, and I believe Katori works at the University of Tokyo, so that connection should be considered for B031; I have no documented collaboration with Katori or Ye. Göran Johansson is my Chalmers colleague, and he directs a centre related to B016, which is not my own conflict but is worth noting when weighing that candidate.
